newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan delays convoy's departure to Central Asia.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan delays convoy's departure to Central Asia.

text.p: Pakistan, eager to build trade ties with oil-rich Central Asian states, has postponed the departure of a planned truck convoy to the Kazakh capital Almaty, an official said on Monday.
Project coordinator Zafar Iqbal Raja told Reuters that 20 trucks carrying rice, wheat and leather goods, would leave from the city of Rawalpindi, near Islamabad, on October 31.
The overland convoy had originally been due to leave on Monday from the southern port city of Karachi.
Raja said the plans had been changed because traders had asked for more time to complete their paper work.
He said the convoy was expected to return to Karachi after 27 days, accompanied by 60 more trucks, 20 each from China, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan.

The convoy's tortous route, trundling up the mountainous Karakoram Highway and across the Khunjerab Pass to the Chinese market town of Kashgar and on to the Kyrgyz capital Bishkek before winding up in Almaty, is expected to take nine days.
Raja said the traders had been given five days to unload their cargo and load new goods for the 13-day return journey.
Strife in Afghanistan, across which the most direct access routes run, has long foiled Pakistani ambitions to promote Karachi as a port serving landlocked Central Asian countries.
Pakistan sent a convoy through Afghanistan in October 1994 to open a trade route with Turkmenistan, but Afghan guerrilla commanders seized the trucks in the southern city of Kandahar.
The radical Islamic Taleban, then virtually unknown, rescued the convoy, routed the local commanders and captured Kandahar, now their headquarters. The convoy finally got through.

Pakistan, China, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan agreed in 1994 to encourage trade by improving the 1,284-km (798-mile) Karakoram highway, completed by Chinese engineers and Pakistani troops in 1978. The trade convoy to Almaty has been planned since June.
The four countries also agreed not to levy transport charges on each other in excess of those levied on their own nationals.
